title: On Biblical Theology
subtitle: The whole Bible as one story that ends in Christ
blurb: Essays tracing the Bible as one story climaxing in Christ — the kingdom of God, exodus, covenant, the image of God, and living between the already and the not yet.

chapters.title: Already and Not Yet: Living Between Two Worlds
chapters.summary: The reason your faith so often feels like victory and defeat at the same time is not that you are doing it wrong but that you are living in the exact overlap the New Testament said you would.
chapters.body:
Every honest believer eventually runs into the same wall. The promises sound total. The new life, the freedom from sin, the peace that surpasses understanding, the defeat of death. And then you wake up the next morning and you are still anxious, still fighting the same old habit, still standing at gravesides. So which is it. Either the promises are exaggerated, or you are failing to claim them. Most of us oscillate between those two conclusions, blaming the Bible one week and ourselves the next. There is a third possibility, and it is the truest thing the New Testament ever taught about the present moment.

The third possibility has a name. Already and not yet. The phrase belongs to George Eldon Ladd, who spent his career arguing that the New Testament holds two truths together that we keep trying to separate, that the kingdom of God has genuinely arrived in Jesus and has not yet arrived in fullness, and that the entire Christian life is lived in the overlap between those two facts (Ladd 1974). You are not crazy. You are not uniquely failing. You are living in the overlap of the ages, where the new creation has begun and the old order has not finished dying, and both are true at the same time, in the same body, on the same Tuesday.

Let the strongest objection have its say, because it is the objection of every clear-eyed person who has watched Christians make excuses. The skeptic says this already-and-not-yet business is just theology covering its own failures. Whatever the gospel promised but did not deliver gets filed under not yet, and whatever it managed to produce gets filed under already, and the scheme is unfalsifiable, a way of always being right by never being checkable. This is a fair charge, and it would be devastating if the structure were invented after the fact to explain disappointment. The question is whether already and not yet is a patch applied to a leaking theory, or whether it was built into the gospel from the start.

It was built in from the start, and the proof is that the New Testament writers describe the tension as the normal condition before anyone needed an excuse for it. Paul does not stumble into already-and-not-yet when his churches disappoint him. He builds his whole understanding of the present on it. 'If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away, behold, the new has come' (2 Corinthians 5:17 ESV). That is the already, stated without hedging. The old is gone. The new is here. And the same Paul, in the same body of letters, writes that the whole creation groans, and we ourselves groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption, the redemption of our bodies (Romans 8:23 ESV). We have been adopted, and we are waiting to be adopted. We are new, and we are groaning. He says both without embarrassment because both are true, and he knew it before any church gave him a reason to need it.

Here is the text I want to carry through, because it holds the whole tension in a single sentence and refuses to release it. Paul writes that God 'raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus' (Ephesians 2:6 ESV). Read that slowly. Seated. Past tense. Already. In the mind of God your future is so certain that he speaks of it as finished. You are already seated with Christ in glory. And then turn a few pages and the same letter tells you to put on the whole armor of God, because you are in a war that is very much still being fought (Ephesians 6:11 ESV). Seated in glory. Armed for battle. The same person, in the same letter, at the same moment. This is not contradiction. This is the shape of the overlap, and once you see it you stop trying to choose between the two halves of your own experience.

The history of the church is largely a history of refusing the overlap, collapsing it toward one side or the other. Some collapse it toward the already. The triumphalist insists you can have it all now, perfect health, unbroken victory, sin behind you forever, and when reality contradicts him he blames the sufferer for lacking faith. This is cruelty dressed as confidence, and it has broken people I have sat with, who were told their cancer was a failure of belief. Others collapse it toward the not yet. The defeatist concludes nothing really changes until heaven, so the present is just grim endurance, and the new creation language is spiritualized into a someday with no purchase on now. Augustine, writing as Rome fell around him, refused both errors. He described two cities intermingled in this present age, the city of God and the city of man, growing up together, not to be separated until the end, so that the Christian lives as a citizen of one city while residing in the other, neither already home nor entirely in exile (Augustine, City of God). He would not let the believer pretend the kingdom had fully come, and he would not let him pretend it had not come at all.

Now the cross, because the overlap is not an abstract scheme. It is carved into the gospel events themselves. At the cross the decisive battle was won. The text says Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15 ESV). The victory is real, and it is past, and it is total. And yet the defeated powers still thrash. This is why the New Testament so often uses the language of an enemy already beaten who has not yet surrendered. Oscar Cullmann gave the picture that has never been improved, the difference between the decisive battle and the final armistice, between D-Day and V-Day (Cullmann 1951). The war was decided on a single day. The fighting continued after, real fighting, real casualties, but the outcome was no longer in doubt. That is exactly where we live. The cross was the day the war was decided. We are in the mopping-up, where the bullets are real and the result is certain.

Watch the reversal. The skeptic said the not-yet was an excuse for the gospel's failures. But the not-yet is not the gospel's weakness, it is the gospel's mercy, the same mercy we met in the kingdom delayed. If the already were complete, if the final reckoning had come the moment Christ rose, then the door would have shut, and it would have shut on you and on me before we ever heard the news. The reason the new creation has begun but not finished is that the King is holding the field open, leaving time for the war's stragglers to come over to the winning side. The very gap the skeptic counts against the gospel is the room in which the skeptic is still being invited in. The not-yet is not a failure to deliver. It is a refusal to slam the door.

So how do we live in the overlap, between the two worlds, seated and armed at once. We live without the two lies the collapse always produces. We refuse the lie of the triumphalist, that says if you suffer you have failed, because the not-yet is real and your groaning is not unbelief, it is honesty. And we refuse the lie of the defeatist, that says nothing changes until you die, because the already is real and the new creation has genuinely begun in you, and the habit you are fighting is a defeated enemy, not an undefeated one. The overlap is not a comfortable place. It was never meant to be. It is a war you fight as a soldier whose victory is already certified, grieving real losses with real hope, refusing both the false peace and the false despair.

That is the verdict, and it does not resolve, because the overlap by definition does not resolve, not yet. You will feel like a new creation and a groaning captive on the same morning, and both readings will be accurate, and the gospel does not ask you to pick one. It asks you to hold them the way Paul did, seated in glory with the armor still on. The war is won. The fighting is real. And the only people who lose their footing in this strange middle country are the ones who insist on living in only one of the two worlds the gospel says we now inhabit together.

### Works Cited

Augustine of Hippo. The City of God. c. 426.

Cullmann, Oscar. Christ and Time: The Primitive Christian Conception of Time and History. London: SCM Press, 1951.

Ladd, George Eldon. A Theology of the New Testament. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1974.

chapters.title: Evolution and Genesis: A Pastor's Guide
chapters.summary: The debate over evolution and Genesis has generated more heat than light for over a century. The path forward requires understanding what Genesis actually says, what science actually shows, and what is genuinely at stake theologically.
chapters.body:
No topic in the conversation between faith and culture has been more badly handled than the relationship between evolution and Genesis. It has been turned into a litmus test for orthodoxy, a battleground for culture wars, and a stumbling block that has driven countless thoughtful people away from the church — not because they could not believe in God but because they were told that believing in God required them to reject the overwhelming consensus of modern science. That is a false choice, and the church should stop offering it.

I say this as a pastor, not as a scientist. My training is in theology, not biology. But I have spent enough time in this debate to know that the options are more numerous, more carefully reasoned, and more theologically responsible than most churches acknowledge. The purpose of this essay is not to tell you what to believe about evolution and Genesis. It is to lay out the terrain honestly so that you can make an informed decision — and to insist that the decision is not between faith and science. It is between different ways of holding both.

What Genesis 1-3 Actually Says

The first step in this conversation is to read Genesis 1-3 carefully, on its own terms, in its own context. This is harder than it sounds, because most of us come to Genesis with centuries of interpretive assumptions already in place — assumptions we mistake for the text itself.

Genesis 1 is a carefully structured, symmetrical text. It describes creation in six days arranged in two parallel triads. In days 1-3, God creates the domains: light and darkness, sky and sea, land and vegetation. In days 4-6, God fills the domains: sun and moon and stars (filling the domain of light), birds and fish (filling sky and sea), land animals and humans (filling the land). Day 7 is the Sabbath — God's rest. The structure is architectural, not chronological. It reads like a liturgical hymn, not a laboratory notebook.

When Genesis 1 is read alongside the other creation texts of the ancient Near East — the Babylonian Enuma Elish, the Egyptian creation accounts, the Atrahasis epic — its distinctive theological claims come into sharp focus. Unlike the Babylonian account, in which the world is created from the dismembered body of a slain goddess, Genesis depicts creation as the free, intentional act of a single God who speaks the world into being. Unlike the Mesopotamian accounts, in which humans are created as slaves to serve the gods, Genesis declares humans to be created in the "image of God" — a royal designation in the ancient world, applied in other cultures only to kings. Genesis is making claims about who God is, what humans are, and what creation means. Whether it is also making claims about how many hours the process took is a question the text itself does not obviously answer.

Genesis 2 tells a different creation story with a different sequence. In Genesis 1, the sequence is vegetation, animals, humans (male and female together). In Genesis 2, the sequence is the man, vegetation, animals, the woman. If both chapters are read as chronological accounts of the same events, they contradict each other. The early church fathers — including Origen, Augustine, and Basil — were aware of this, and none of them treated both accounts as straightforward chronological history. Augustine, in The Literal Meaning of Genesis, argued that the "days" of creation might not be ordinary days and that Christians should not make claims about the natural world that would make the faith look foolish to educated pagans. That was in the fifth century.

Young Earth Creationism

Young Earth Creationism (YEC) holds that Genesis 1-2 describes the creation of the universe in six literal twenty-four-hour days, approximately 6,000 to 10,000 years ago. The position is associated with the work of Henry Morris and John Whitcomb, whose The Genesis Flood (1961) launched the modern young-earth movement, and with organizations like Answers in Genesis, the Institute for Creation Research, and the Creation Research Society.

YEC proponents argue that the Hebrew word yom (day), when accompanied by a number and the phrase "evening and morning," always refers to a literal twenty-four-hour day in the Old Testament. They argue that the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 provide a chronological framework that, when calculated, yields an age for the earth of roughly 6,000 years. They argue that the geological record is better explained by a global flood than by uniformitarian geology, and that the apparent age of the universe — the light from distant stars, the radiometric dating of rocks, the fossil record — is either the result of God creating the universe with the appearance of age or the product of catastrophic geological processes during and after the flood.

The scientific difficulties with YEC are substantial and well-documented. The age of the universe — 13.8 billion years, established by multiple independent lines of evidence including cosmic microwave background radiation, the redshift of distant galaxies, and the abundance of light elements — is not a marginal finding. It is one of the best-established results in all of science. The age of the earth — 4.5 billion years, established by radiometric dating of meteorites and terrestrial rocks — is similarly well-established. The fossil record documents the sequential appearance of life forms over hundreds of millions of years, in a pattern that is consistent with evolutionary theory and inconsistent with the simultaneous creation of all species. To reject these findings requires rejecting not a single scientific claim but the entire framework of modern physics, chemistry, geology, and biology.

This does not mean that people who hold YEC are unintelligent. Many are deeply thoughtful. But the scientific case against a young earth is overwhelming, and the church does itself no favors by pretending otherwise.

Old Earth Creationism

Old Earth Creationism (OEC) accepts the scientific evidence for the age of the universe and the earth while maintaining that God created the major kinds of life through direct, special creative acts. The position takes several forms.

The day-age interpretation reads the "days" of Genesis 1 as long periods of time — eons rather than twenty-four-hour days. The Hebrew word yom can refer to an indefinite period (as in "the day of the Lord"), and proponents argue that this reading is linguistically legitimate and aligns the Genesis sequence roughly with the scientific sequence of cosmic and biological history. Hugh Ross, an astrophysicist and the founder of Reasons to Believe, is the most prominent advocate of this view.

The gap theory posits a long interval between Genesis 1:1 ("In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth") and Genesis 1:2 ("The earth was without form and void"), during which the geological ages unfolded. The six days of creation in Genesis 1:3-31 describe a relatively recent re-creation or restoration of the earth. This view was popular in the nineteenth century but has largely fallen out of favor among both scientists and theologians.

The framework interpretation, developed by Meredith Kline and Henri Blocher, reads the six days of Genesis 1 not as a chronological sequence but as a literary framework — a topical arrangement that presents God's creative work in two parallel triads (forming and filling). On this view, the "days" are a literary device, not a calendar, and the question of how long creation took is simply not a question Genesis is designed to answer.

Evolutionary Creation

Evolutionary creation (also called theistic evolution) accepts the full scientific account of evolution — common descent, natural selection, deep time — while affirming that the entire process is God's chosen method of creation. On this view, God did not create each species individually by direct intervention. God created a universe with the physical laws and initial conditions necessary for life to emerge and evolve, and God sustains and directs the process through natural means. Evolution is not an alternative to divine creation. It is the mechanism of divine creation.

The BioLogos Foundation, founded by Francis Collins, is the most prominent advocate of evolutionary creation. Denis Lamoureux, a professor of science and religion at the University of Alberta, has developed a sophisticated theological framework for the position, arguing that just as God accommodated divine revelation to the scientific understanding of the biblical authors (who assumed a flat earth and a solid dome over the sky), so God accommodated the mechanism of creation to natural processes that science can investigate.

Evolutionary creationists argue that the evidence for common descent is overwhelming: the shared DNA of all living organisms, the nested hierarchy of morphological similarities, the fossil record's documentation of transitional forms, the geographic distribution of species, the vestigial structures that make no sense apart from evolutionary history. They argue that this evidence is not a threat to faith but a source of wonder — that the God who could create a universe capable of generating life, consciousness, and love through the patient unfolding of natural processes is a more impressive God, not a lesser one.

What Is at Stake Theologically

The real theological questions in the evolution debate are not about the age of the earth or the mechanism of speciation. They are about deeper matters: the image of God, the fall, original sin, and the nature of death.

If human beings evolved from earlier primates, what does it mean to say that humans are created in the "image of God"? The answer depends on what the image of God is. If it is a biological feature — a soul implanted in the first human pair at a specific moment in history — then evolutionary continuity with other species poses a challenge. But if the image of God is a relational and vocational category — the capacity to relate to God, to bear God's authority in creation, to exercise stewardship and moral responsibility — then it need not be located in a specific biological event. It can be understood as a divine calling conferred on humanity as humanity emerged into the kind of consciousness that could receive it.

The fall is a more difficult question. If there was no historical Adam and Eve, no single moment of first disobedience in a garden, what do we make of the doctrine of original sin? Several options have been proposed. Some evolutionary creationists argue that Adam and Eve were historical figures — perhaps the first members of a population of early humans whom God called into covenant relationship. Others argue that the fall is a theological description of a universal human condition — the pervasive tendency toward selfishness, idolatry, and violence that characterizes every human society — rather than a historical account of a single event. The apostle Paul's use of Adam in Romans 5 must be taken seriously, but Paul's theological point — that sin and death are universal, and that Christ is the answer to both — does not necessarily depend on a particular theory of human origins.

The question of death before the fall is also significant. If the earth is billions of years old and life has been evolving for hundreds of millions of years, then death — animal death, at a minimum — preceded any human sin. YEC proponents argue that this contradicts Romans 5:12 ("sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin"). But many scholars argue that Paul's reference is to human death, not animal death, and that the natural death of organisms is a feature of a good creation, not a consequence of the fall. Trees shedding leaves, predators consuming prey, organisms completing their life cycles — these are not evils to be explained. They are the normal operations of a living world.

How to Have This Conversation Honestly

The evolution-and-Genesis debate generates more heat than light because both sides often fight for things that are not actually at stake. The young-earth creationist fears that accepting evolution means abandoning the authority of Scripture, the reality of God's creative action, and the theological significance of human beings. These fears are understandable, but they are not warranted. One can affirm the authority of Scripture, the reality of divine creation, and the unique dignity of human beings while accepting the scientific evidence for evolution. The question is not whether God created. The question is how.

The secularist, on the other hand, often assumes that evolution disproves God — that the mechanism of natural selection, once understood, eliminates the need for a Creator. This is a philosophical claim, not a scientific one. Natural selection explains how species change over time. It does not explain why there is a universe capable of producing life in the first place, or why that universe is governed by the kind of mathematical laws that make science possible, or why consciousness emerged from matter, or why human beings experience moral obligation. Evolution is a powerful explanation of biological diversity. It is not a metaphysical system.

The church owes its people better than a false choice between faith and science. It owes them the truth: that the Christian tradition has always contained a diversity of views on how to read Genesis, that the greatest minds in the history of the church did not read Genesis 1 as a science textbook, and that the theological convictions that matter — that God is the Creator, that the universe is not an accident, that human beings bear the image of God and are called to a purpose — can be held with integrity regardless of one's view on the mechanism of creation.

What cannot be held with integrity is the insistence that Christians must choose between their Bibles and their biology textbooks. That insistence is not a defense of the faith. It is an obstacle to it. And it is time the church stopped building obstacles and started building bridges — not by abandoning theological conviction, but by distinguishing conviction from interpretation, and interpretation from the Word of God itself.

chapters.title: Exodus: The Story Underneath the Whole Bible
chapters.summary: Every act of rescue in Scripture is told in the grammar of one ancient escape from Egypt, and until you learn that grammar you will keep mistaking the gospel for something smaller than freedom.
chapters.body:
Israel did not begin its national memory with a creed. It began with a rescue. When a later generation asked what it meant to belong to this God, the answer was not a definition. It was a story. 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery' (Exodus 20:2 ESV). That sentence stands at the head of the Ten Commandments. Before God gives a single command, he names himself by what he did. He is the God who got his people out.

We tend to read Exodus as one episode among many, a dramatic chapter with plagues and a parted sea, useful for children's films. That is a failure of attention. Exodus is not an episode. It is the template. It is the shape every later rescue in Scripture is poured into, the deep grammar of how God saves. Christopher Wright argues that the exodus functions as the paradigm of redemption for the entire Hebrew Bible, the event Israel reached for whenever it needed to understand what salvation was (Wright 2006). When the prophets imagine a future deliverance, they describe a new exodus. When the psalmist needs to praise, he rehearses the sea. The story underneath the whole Bible is the story of a God who hears slaves and comes down.

Look at how it actually begins, because the beginning is the part we rush past. It does not begin with a plan. It begins with a sound. 'The people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. And their cry for help came up to God. And God heard their groaning' (Exodus 2:23-24 ESV). Before there is a Moses, before there is a bush, there is a groan that reaches heaven. This is the first thing Exodus wants us to know about God, and it is the thing we least believe when we are the ones groaning. He hears. The text is almost monotonous about it. God heard, God remembered, God saw, God knew. Four verbs, and salvation has not yet visibly moved, but the whole outcome is already certain, because God has turned his face toward the noise of suffering.

Now consider the strongest objection, the one a thoughtful skeptic raises and a grieving believer feels in the night. If this God hears groaning and comes down to rescue, where is he. The slaves in Egypt cried for four centuries before the sea opened. The objection is not that God never acts. It is that he is unbearably slow, and that the gap between the groan and the rescue is filled with real children who died still enslaved. Walter Brueggemann does not flinch from this. He notes that the exodus is precisely a story told by people who knew exile, who knew what it was to wait on a God whose timing they could not control or excuse (Brueggemann 1997). The honest reading of Exodus does not promise that rescue is prompt. It promises that rescue is real, and that the waiting is not the same as abandonment.

What the objection gets right is the cost of the delay. Scripture never sanitizes it. But the shape of the story answers the objection in a way no argument could. The exodus tells us that God's silence is not God's absence, because the same God who waited four centuries was, the whole time, hearing. The groan was already filed in heaven. The rescue was already coming before the rescuer was born. The slowness we read as neglect, the story reads as a God working below the surface of a history that looks God-forsaken.

Then comes the night that names everything. Because here is the part of the exodus we sentimentalize most and understand least. The final plague does not pass over Israel because Israel was innocent. The destroyer comes for every firstborn in the land, and the only difference between a saved house and a bereaved one is blood on a doorframe. 'The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you' (Exodus 12:13 ESV). A lamb dies so that a household lives. This is the diagnosis before the deliverance, the law before the grace. Israel is not rescued because Israel deserved it more than Egypt. Israel is rescued because a substitute bled in the doorway. The exodus is not a story about good people escaping bad people. It is a story about death passing over a people who had done nothing to earn the lamb.

That is the spine that runs to the cross. The Gospels are not subtle about it. Jesus goes to Jerusalem to die at Passover, the very feast that remembers the lamb. John the Baptist sees him coming and says, 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world' (John 1:29 ESV). Paul writes flatly that Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7 ESV). The New Testament reads the cross through Exodus on purpose, because the cross is the exodus the first one was always pointing toward. Egypt was never the real captor. The real captor was the sin and death that hold every human being, Egyptian and Israelite, in the same chains. And the rescue from that captivity costs the same currency it always cost. A lamb in the doorway. A firstborn who dies so the household lives. Only this time the lamb is the firstborn, and the doorway is a Roman cross, and the blood is the blood of God's own Son.

Now watch the reversal turn. The skeptic's question, where is the God who rescues, is answered not by a God who stays safely above the suffering and pulls his favorites out of it. It is answered by a God who climbs down into the slavery himself. The cross is the exodus where the deliverer does not stand on the far shore waving the slaves across. He becomes the lamb. He takes the place in the doorway. The question, why is God so slow to come down, meets the answer that he came all the way down, lower than Egypt, into the grave itself, and came out the other side leading captives free. The delay you held against him was the long road he was walking toward you the whole time.

And notice what the rescued are rescued for, because this is where most of our gospel goes thin. Israel is not brought out of Egypt to wander free in a vague liberty. They are brought out to Sinai, and from Sinai to a land, and at the center of the land a tabernacle, so that God can dwell among them. The exodus ends not with an escape but with a presence. 'Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst' (Exodus 25:8 ESV). Freedom in the Bible is never merely freedom from. It is freedom for. Out of slavery, into the presence of God. The whole arc bends toward the last pages of Scripture, where the new exodus is complete and the voice from the throne says the dwelling place of God is with man, and he will dwell with them (Revelation 21:3 ESV). The exodus was always heading home.

So we read our own bondage by this light, and we should be careful here, because the exodus refuses both the lie that says we are not enslaved and the lie that says we can free ourselves. Egypt is not only a place in the past. It is the name for whatever holds a human being against the purpose of God, the habit you cannot break, the fear you organize your life around, the resentment you nurse, the self you cannot put down. We do not march out of those by trying harder. No slave ever escaped Egypt by improving his attitude toward Pharaoh. The exodus comes from outside. It comes from a God who hears the groan we are often too defeated even to pray.

That is the story underneath the whole Bible. Not advice. Rescue. A God who hears slaves, comes down into their misery, provides the lamb, leads them through the water, and brings them home to himself. We did not begin with a creed, and neither did Israel. We began in a doorway, in the dark, with the destroyer abroad in the land, listening to the breathing of a household that should have died and did not, because something else died in its place. Whoever understands that night understands everything that comes after it.

### Works Cited

Brueggemann, Walter. Theology of the Old Testament. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1997.

Wright, Christopher J.H. The Mission of God. Downers Grove: IVP Academic, 2006.

chapters.title: Science and Faith Are Not at War
chapters.summary: The supposed war between science and religion is not a historical fact but a nineteenth-century invention — and the real history is far more interesting than the myth it replaced.
chapters.body:
The narrative is so deeply embedded in Western culture that it feels like a fact: science and religion have always been at war, and science has been winning. The narrative has its canonical stories — Galileo persecuted by the Inquisition, Darwin demolishing Genesis, Copernicus defying the church — and its implicit moral: as scientific knowledge advances, religious belief retreats, because the two are fundamentally incompatible. One deals in evidence; the other in wishful thinking. One progresses; the other regresses. The choice between them is a choice between reason and superstition.

This narrative is largely false. It is not false because the church has always been friendly to science — it has not. It is false because the relationship between science and faith is far more complex, far more collaborative, and far more interesting than the warfare metaphor allows. The conflict thesis, as historians of science call it, was itself an invention — a nineteenth-century polemical construction that serious historians have spent the last several decades dismantling.

The Conflict Thesis and Its Collapse

The idea that science and religion are inherently at war was popularized by two books: John William Draper's History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science (1874) and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896). Both were enormously influential. Both were also deeply misleading. Draper and White had agendas — Draper was an anti-Catholic polemicist, and White was the president of Cornell University, which he had founded as a secular institution and needed to defend against religious critics. Their books were not dispassionate histories. They were advocacy documents dressed in historical clothing.

The conflict thesis has been rejected by virtually every serious historian of science working today. David Lindberg and Ronald Numbers, in their landmark edited volume God and Nature: Historical Essays on the Encounter Between Christianity and Science (1986), demonstrated that the relationship between Christianity and the natural sciences has been characterized far more by complexity, collaboration, and mutual influence than by conflict. John Hedley Brooke's Science and Religion: Some Historical Perspectives (1991) came to the same conclusion. The consensus among historians of science is clear: the warfare metaphor is a myth.

This does not mean there have been no conflicts. There have been real and significant episodes of tension between scientific findings and theological claims. But these episodes have been the exception, not the rule, and even the canonical examples — Galileo, Darwin — are far more complicated than the popular versions suggest.

What Actually Happened with Galileo

The Galileo affair is the founding myth of the conflict narrative: a courageous scientist persecuted by an ignorant church for daring to assert that the earth moves around the sun. The actual history is considerably more tangled.

Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) was a devout Catholic who never abandoned his faith. His heliocentric views, published in Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632), drew on the work of Copernicus — who was himself a Catholic canon, and whose De Revolutionibus (1543) had been dedicated to Pope Paul III. The Copernican system had circulated for decades without provoking significant ecclesiastical opposition. Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, the most prominent theologian of the era, had stated explicitly that if heliocentrism were scientifically demonstrated, the church would need to reinterpret the relevant biblical passages.

What turned the Galileo case from a scientific debate into a confrontation was a combination of personal politics, ecclesiastical power dynamics, and Galileo's own rhetorical missteps. Galileo's Dialogue placed the geocentric arguments in the mouth of a character named Simplicio — a name that could be read as "simpleton" — and Pope Urban VIII, who had previously been Galileo's patron, believed that Simplicio's arguments were a caricature of his own views. The prosecution of Galileo was driven as much by wounded pride and political calculation as by theological conviction. The Inquisition's condemnation was real, and it was wrong. But it was not a case of science versus religion in any straightforward sense. It was a case of institutional power, personal animosity, and theological overreach — a failure of the church to distinguish between the Bible's theological message and the cosmological assumptions of its authors.

Darwin and the Church: The Actual Record

The popular narrative of Darwin's reception is similarly oversimplified. The story usually told goes like this: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, the church reacted with horror, and the famous debate between Thomas Henry Huxley and Bishop Samuel Wilberforce at Oxford in 1860 settled the matter in science's favor. The actual history is far more diverse.

Many Christians — including prominent theologians and clergy — accepted evolution relatively quickly. Asa Gray, the foremost American botanist and a devout Christian, was Darwin's most important ally in the United States and saw no conflict between evolution and faith. Charles Kingsley, an Anglican clergyman and novelist, wrote to Darwin that it was "just as noble a conception of Deity to believe that He created primal forms capable of self-development" as to believe in special creation. B.B. Warfield, the Princeton theologian most associated with the doctrine of biblical inerrancy, accepted a form of theistic evolution — a fact that would astonish many of his modern admirers.

The Huxley-Wilberforce debate, far from being the decisive confrontation of popular memory, was actually a minor event at the time. The story was embellished and mythologized in subsequent decades, largely by Huxley's allies, to serve the narrative of science's triumph over religion. Contemporary accounts of the debate are inconsistent — witnesses disagreed about what was said, who won, and whether the exchange was as dramatic as later versions claimed.

The opposition to Darwin that did exist came not only from religious quarters. Many scientists — including figures like Lord Kelvin, who objected on thermodynamic grounds, and St. George Jackson Mivart, who offered scientific criticisms of natural selection — resisted Darwin's theory on scientific, not religious, grounds. The debate over evolution in the nineteenth century was genuinely complex. The reduction of that complexity to "science versus religion" is a distortion of the historical record.

Christians and the History of Science

The conflict thesis obscures one of the most remarkable features of the history of science: the central role that Christian institutions and Christian thinkers played in the development of the scientific enterprise. The medieval university system — the institutional framework within which modern science emerged — was a creation of the church. The University of Paris, the University of Oxford, the University of Bologna — all were founded under ecclesiastical authority in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The monks and clerics who populated these institutions were not enemies of learning. They were its custodians.

The list of scientists who were devout Christians is not a list of exceptions. It is a catalog of the founders of modern science. Copernicus was a Catholic canon. Galileo remained a Catholic throughout his life. Johannes Kepler described his astronomical work as "thinking God's thoughts after him." Isaac Newton wrote more pages of theology than of physics. Gregor Mendel, the founder of genetics, was an Augustinian friar. Georges Lemaitre, who proposed the Big Bang theory, was a Catholic priest. The assumption that scientific genius and religious belief are incompatible is contradicted by the very history of science itself.

The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead argued in Science and the Modern World (1925) that modern science was made possible by the medieval conviction, rooted in Christian theology, that the universe is rational and ordered — that it operates according to consistent laws because it is the creation of a rational God. This conviction, Whitehead argued, provided the philosophical foundation for the scientific method: the belief that the universe is intelligible, that its patterns can be discovered, and that the human mind is equipped to discover them. Without this conviction, the enterprise of science would have no warrant.

Scientists Who Believe

The claim that serious scientists cannot be serious believers is refuted by the existence of serious scientists who are serious believers. Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project and served as director of the National Institutes of Health, is an evangelical Christian who has written extensively about the compatibility of faith and science. John Polkinghorne, a Cambridge particle physicist who became an Anglican priest, developed a sophisticated theology of science that integrates quantum mechanics and trinitarian theology. Jennifer Wiseman, a senior astrophysicist at NASA, has spoken publicly about how her study of the cosmos deepens rather than diminishes her Christian faith.

A 2009 Pew Research Center survey found that 51 percent of scientists believe in God or a higher power. The number is lower than the general population, but it is not negligible — and it demolishes the claim that scientific expertise is incompatible with religious belief. The National Academy of Sciences includes members who are devout Christians, Jews, Muslims, and adherents of other traditions. They do not check their faith at the laboratory door.

Models for the Relationship

If science and faith are not at war, what is their relationship? Several models have been proposed, each with strengths and limitations.

Stephen Jay Gould proposed the NOMA model — Non-Overlapping Magisteria — in his 1999 book Rocks of Ages. On this view, science and religion address fundamentally different questions: science asks how the natural world works; religion asks what it means and how we should live. The two domains do not overlap, and conflict arises only when one trespasses on the other's territory. The NOMA model has the virtue of clarity, but many thinkers — both scientific and theological — find it too neat. If God created the universe, then God's creative action must have some relationship to the universe that science studies. And if science discovers features of the universe that bear on questions of meaning — the fine-tuning of cosmological constants, the emergence of consciousness — then the magisteria do overlap, whether we want them to or not.

The dialogue model, associated with Ian Barbour and others, holds that science and religion address different questions but that their answers interact and can inform each other. Scientific discoveries about the age of the universe, the evolution of life, and the nature of consciousness raise questions that theology has resources to address. Theological convictions about the goodness of creation, the value of human life, and the reality of moral obligation raise questions that science alone cannot answer. The two disciplines are in conversation, not competition.

The integration model goes further, arguing that science and theology can be woven into a single, coherent framework. Teilhard de Chardin, the Jesuit paleontologist, attempted a grand synthesis of evolutionary biology and Christian theology. More recently, scholars associated with the John Templeton Foundation have pursued research at the intersection of science and religion, exploring questions about the nature of consciousness, the fine-tuning of the cosmos, and the evolutionary origins of altruism.

No single model captures the full complexity of the relationship. What all serious models share is the rejection of the warfare metaphor — the recognition that science and faith, whatever their tensions, are not enemies but neighbors, occupying adjacent rooms in the house of human inquiry, and that the conversation between them is one of the most important conversations a thoughtful person can have.

The Questions Science Cannot Answer

The limits of science are not weaknesses. They are the boundaries of a discipline that has defined its domain with admirable precision. Science investigates the natural world through observation, hypothesis, experimentation, and revision. It does this extraordinarily well. But there are questions that the scientific method, by its own design, is not equipped to answer. Why is there something rather than nothing? What grounds moral obligation? Does life have purpose? Is the universe meaningful, or is meaning a human projection onto an indifferent cosmos? What happens when we die?

These are not failed scientific questions waiting for better instruments. They are philosophical and theological questions that require different tools — tools that include reason, tradition, experience, revelation, and the cumulative wisdom of communities that have wrestled with these questions for millennia. The scientist who says "science cannot answer that question" is not confessing a limitation. The scientist is defining a boundary. And the theologian who says "let me bring a different set of tools to the table" is not trespassing on science's territory. The theologian is working in an adjacent field where the soil is different and the methods must be different too.

The deepest mistake of the new atheism — the movement associated with Richard Dawkins, Sam Harris, Christopher Hitchens, and Daniel Dennett — was not its criticism of religion's failures, much of which was deserved. The deepest mistake was its claim that science could replace religion — that empirical investigation could answer every meaningful human question, and that any question science could not answer was therefore not a real question. This is not a scientific claim. It is a philosophical claim — the claim known as scientism — and it is a claim that most philosophers, including many who are atheists, regard as unjustified. Science is magnificent at telling us how the universe works. It has nothing to say about whether the universe matters.

The war between science and faith is not a war that needs to be won. It is a war that never existed — except in the imagination of polemicists on both sides who found it more useful to fight than to think. The actual history is richer, messier, and more hopeful than the myth. And the sooner we leave the myth behind, the sooner we can get on with the real work: asking the deepest questions about the universe with every tool we have — including both the telescope and the prayer.

chapters.title: What Is the Kingdom of God
chapters.summary: The kingdom of God is not a place you go when you die and not a program you build with your own hands, and once you see what it actually is, you cannot read the rest of the Bible the same way.
chapters.body:
A man walks out of the wilderness in a backwater province of the Roman Empire, and the first thing out of his mouth is a sentence that does not sound like good news to anyone listening. 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand. Repent and believe in the gospel' (Mark 1:14-15 ESV). Mark gives us no childhood, no genealogy, no slow build. He drops us into motion. And the first word Jesus preaches is not love, not grace, not even God. The first word is kingdom.

We have spent two thousand years making that word smaller than it is. Ask the average person in the pew what the kingdom of God means and you will get one of three answers, and each of them is a ruin of the original. Some will say it means heaven, the place your soul travels to after death. Some will say it means a better society, the cause you organize for, the politics you bless. Some will say it means a feeling, an inner peace, the territory of the private heart. Each of these contains a fragment of the truth. None of them is the thing. And the gap between the fragment and the thing is where most of our discipleship quietly dies.

Start with the word itself, because the word has been mistranslated in our imaginations. The Greek is basileia. Behind it stands the Hebrew malkuth. Neither word primarily means a territory. They mean reign, rule, the active exercise of kingship. George Eldon Ladd spent his career pressing this single point against a church that kept hearing real estate where the text said sovereignty (Ladd 1959). The kingdom of God is not first a where. It is a happening. It is God stepping into the world to be king of it again. When Jesus says the kingdom is at hand, he is not announcing the address of the afterlife. He is announcing an invasion.

The word also carries a history older than Jesus, and the history matters, because his hearers did not come to that sermon with empty ears. For centuries Israel had sung the malkuth of God in its worship. The Lord reigns, the psalms declared, let the earth rejoice (Psalm 97:1 ESV). But to sing that God reigns while Babylon burned your temple and Rome posted soldiers in your streets was to sing against the visible evidence. The kingship of God had become a contested claim, a hope held in the teeth of an occupation. So when a Galilean stood up and said the reign of God was now at hand, he was not introducing a novel idea. He was lighting a fuse that had been laid centuries before, and everyone within earshot knew what was supposed to happen when that reign finally arrived. The enemies of God would be judged. The exile would end. The world would be set right. That expectation is the pressure behind every page of the Gospels, and we cannot feel the scandal of Jesus until we feel what his hearers were braced for and did not get.

That changes the grammar of the whole Gospel. If the kingdom were a place, the only question would be how to get in. But if the kingdom is God's active reign breaking into history, then the question becomes something far more disturbing. It becomes whether you will surrender to a king who has arrived without your permission. This is why the announcement comes wrapped in a command. Repent. The word is not religious throat-clearing. It is what you do when a true king turns up and you have been living as though the throne were empty.

Consider the strongest version of the objection, because it deserves to be met at full strength. The skeptic, and many honest Christians with him, looks at the world and says the kingdom plainly did not come. Jesus announced God's reign, and then Rome went on ruling, the poor stayed poor, the cross happened, and the centuries since have been a long catalog of war and famine and the church itself often on the wrong side of both. Albert Schweitzer made this case with brutal honesty over a century ago, arguing that Jesus expected the immediate, cataclysmic arrival of the kingdom and was simply wrong, that the wheel of history did not turn and instead crushed him (Schweitzer 1906). This is not a cheap objection. It is the most serious one. If the kingdom came, why does the world look like this.

What the objection gets right is that the kingdom was supposed to be visible. The Hebrew prophets did not dream of a private spirituality. They dreamed of swords beaten into plowshares, of the wolf lying down with the lamb, of a king on David's throne whose government had no end (Isaiah 9:7 ESV). Walter Brueggemann calls this the prophetic imagination, the refusal to accept the present arrangement as final, the insistence that the world owes God an account it has not yet paid (Brueggemann 1978). The skeptic and the prophet agree on one thing the comfortable Christian forgets. If the kingdom is real, it must touch the ground. It must show up in bodies and bread and the actual structures of power. A kingdom that changes nothing visible is not a kingdom. It is a mood.

So we cannot answer Schweitzer by retreating into the inner life. That retreat is exactly the first misreading, the kingdom shrunk to a feeling, and it is a betrayal of everything the prophets meant. Jesus himself blocks that exit. When the Pharisees ask when the kingdom will come, he says the kingdom of God is not coming with signs to be observed, and then, 'the kingdom of God is in the midst of you' (Luke 17:21 ESV). That phrase has been domesticated into 'within you,' as though Jesus were pointing at the human heart. He was not. He was standing in front of them. The kingdom was in their midst because the king was in their midst, eating with them, touching lepers, telling them stories that turned their world inside out. The kingdom is not in your interior. It is in the room, and it has a face.

This is where Ladd's great contribution does its work, and where the false either-or finally breaks. The kingdom has both come and not yet come. Already and not yet. Ladd argued that the New Testament holds two truths in a single grip that we keep trying to pry apart (Ladd 1974). The kingdom is genuinely present. In Jesus the future has invaded the present. When he casts out demons, he says, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Matthew 12:28 ESV). The reign of God is here, in his person, in his acts, like the first light before dawn that is genuinely day even though the sun has not cleared the horizon. And yet the kingdom is also future. We still pray, 'your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven' (Matthew 6:10 ESV). We would not pray for what we already fully possess. The kingdom has come in the king. The kingdom has not yet come in its fullness. We live in the overlap, in the strange and uncomfortable middle, where the decisive battle is won and the war is not over.

This was not the church's settled instinct, and the history of how we lost it is instructive. The earliest believers lived in the tension naturally, expecting the King's return and ordering their common life around it. But across the centuries the two halves of the truth kept tearing apart. By the fourth century, when Constantine made the faith respectable and the empire baptized itself, a powerful temptation arrived to read the kingdom as already arrived in Christendom itself, the church and the state fused into the visible reign of God on earth. Augustine wrote The City of God against exactly that confusion, refusing to identify the kingdom of God with any earthly order, Roman or ecclesial, insisting that the two cities grow up intermingled until the end and are not to be sorted by human hands (Augustine, City of God). He saw what happens when the church mistakes itself for the finished kingdom. It stops praying come and starts policing the borders of a kingdom it imagines it already runs. Augustine's correction held for a time and then was forgotten, and forgotten again, in every age that has tried to build the kingdom by force or announce that we have already arrived.

This is not a clever dodge invented to save Jesus from Schweitzer. It is written into the parables, which are the kingdom's native language. Think of the parables Jesus uses, all of them straining toward this double truth. The kingdom is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, that becomes a tree (Matthew 13:31-32 ESV). It is here, small, easy to miss, and it is going to become enormous, and both things are true at once. The kingdom is like leaven a woman hides in three measures of flour until it is all leavened (Matthew 13:33 ESV). Present, hidden, working, not yet finished. The kingdom is like a man who sows good seed, and then his enemy sows weeds among the wheat, and the master says let them grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24-30 ESV). The kingdom has come, and the weeds are still standing, and the day of sorting is not yet. Jesus answered Schweitzer's objection before Schweitzer was born. The kingdom did come. It came like a seed, not like an army. The visible fullness is held back, on purpose, to leave room for repentance.

This is the reversal, and it is the heart of the matter. The objection, that the kingdom did not arrive in power, is not a refutation of the gospel. It is a description of the mercy of God. The reason the world is not yet swept clean, the reason the wheat and the weeds still grow in the same field, is that the king is patient, not wanting any to perish but all to reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9 ESV). The delay the skeptic counts as evidence against the kingdom is the very space in which the skeptic is being given time to repent. The gap between already and not yet is not a flaw in the system. It is grace, stretched out in time, holding the door open. If the kingdom had come in full the day Jesus announced it, the door would have shut on every one of us. The slowness is the love.

But we have not yet reached the bottom of the announcement, and the bottom is where the cross stands. Because how does this king establish his reign. Not the way Schweitzer expected and not the way the crowd wanted. The crowd wanted a kingdom that would throw out Rome. They wanted the second misreading, the kingdom as political program, the cause that names its enemies and crushes them. Jesus refused it so completely that when they tried to make him king by force, he withdrew (John 6:15 ESV). And then he marched toward Jerusalem and let himself be killed by the very empire everyone wanted him to overthrow.

N.T. Wright has spent decades insisting that we cannot understand the kingdom apart from the cross, that the crucifixion is not a detour from the kingdom project but the means by which the kingdom comes (Wright 1996). On the cross the king does battle with the real enemy, which was never Rome. The real enemy is the sin and death that hold every human being, Roman and Jew, skeptic and saint, in the same grip. The kingdom comes through a throne that is a gallows. The crown is made of thorns. This is the law before the grace, and we have to feel the law first. The reason the kingdom could not simply arrive and fix everything is that the problem was not out there in the structures. The problem was in us. I am the weed in the field. The empire I most need overthrown is the one I administer in my own chest. Until that is dealt with, no rearrangement of the world's furniture will save it. And it could only be dealt with by a king willing to die for his rebels.

Watch how the placard over his head completes the argument. Pilate had it nailed to the cross, written in three languages so no passerby could miss it, the King of the Jews (John 19:19 ESV). It was meant as mockery, a joke at the expense of a beaten man and the nation he failed to deliver. But the Gospels report it because the mockery told the truth Pilate did not understand. This is in fact how this King reigns. The title is accurate. The throne is the cross. The crowd wanted a Messiah who would do to Rome what Rome did to its enemies, and they got instead a King who absorbed the violence rather than dealing it, who let the empire spend its full force on him and exhausted it there. Brueggemann's prophetic imagination reaches its limit and its fulfillment at this point, because the prophets imagined a reign that would overturn the arrangements of power, and here the reign arrives by submitting to the worst those arrangements could do, and breaking them from the inside (Brueggemann 1978). The kingdom does not defeat the violence of the world by out-violencing it. It defeats it by refusing to play, and dying, and rising anyway.

That is why the announcement begins with repent. Not because God is petty about rules, but because the kingdom is the reign of God, and you cannot have the reign of God in a heart that insists on reigning itself. The cross is where the false king in me is dethroned, and the true king takes the throne by the most unlikely conquest in history, by being conquered. The grave could not hold him, and his rising is the first square foot of the new creation, the not-yet breaking decisively into the already, the guarantee that the harvest will come.

Lesslie Newbigin saw what this means for the church with a clarity born of watching the gospel land in cultures that had never heard it. The church, he wrote, is not the kingdom. The church is the sign, the foretaste, the instrument of the kingdom, a community that lives now by the rules of a reign that is not yet visible everywhere, so that the world can see what is coming (Newbigin 1989). When the church forgets this, it makes both of the old mistakes at once. It either becomes a waiting room for heaven, a society of people killing time until they die, which is the kingdom-as-place error. Or it becomes one more political faction baptizing its preferred power, which is the kingdom-as-program error. The true church is stranger than both. It is a colony of the future, planted in the present, that does not match either the despair of the world or the pretensions of the world. It feeds the hungry not to build utopia but because the king it serves does, and it does not despair when the weeds keep growing because it knows whose hand controls the harvest.

Newbigin had earned this by watching it happen. He spent decades in India, where the gospel arrived in a culture that owed it nothing and shared none of its assumptions, and he saw that the kingdom could not be argued into people as an idea. It had to be visible in a community, or it was not credible at all. The only hermeneutic of the gospel, he wrote, the only interpretation the watching world will finally trust, is a congregation that believes it (Newbigin 1989). That is a heavy word for the church, and it should land as conviction before it lands as comfort. If the reign of God is real and present, then the question the world is entitled to ask is not whether our doctrine is coherent. It is whether anything in our common life looks like a place where God is actually king. I have to ask it of my own congregation, and of myself, and the honest answer is rarely the whole answer I would like to give. We are a sign that is often smudged. We are a foretaste that frequently tastes of nothing. And yet the kingdom does not depend on the quality of the sign for its coming, which is the only reason a smudged church can preach it at all.

So what is the kingdom of God. It is the reign of God breaking into history in the person of Jesus, decisively begun and not yet complete, announced in a sermon, demonstrated in healings, parabled in seeds and leaven, won on a cross, sealed in an empty tomb, entrusted to a people, and aimed at a day when the prayer is finally answered and the will of God is done on earth as it is in heaven. It is not where you go. It is who is reigning. And the only question the announcement leaves you is the one it asked from the beginning, standing there in Galilee with the dust still on his feet. The king has come. The throne is no longer empty. What will you do with the fact that it was never yours.

### Works Cited

Augustine of Hippo. The City of God. c. 426.

Brueggemann, Walter. The Prophetic Imagination. Philadelphia: Fortress Press, 1978.

Ladd, George Eldon. The Gospel of the Kingdom. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1959.

Ladd, George Eldon. A Theology of the New Testament. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1974.

Newbigin, Lesslie. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1989.

Schweitzer, Albert. The Quest of the Historical Jesus. London: A. and C. Black, 1906.

Wright, N.T. Jesus and the Victory of God. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1996.

chapters.title: What It Means to Bear the Image of God
chapters.summary: The oldest sentence about human dignity is not that we are smart or useful or productive but that we carry the likeness of God, and everything humane in our civilization is a borrowed inheritance from that one claim.
chapters.body:
The first thing the Bible says about a human being is the most radical thing ever said about one. 'So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them' (Genesis 1:27 ESV). Six chapters of cosmos, light and water and stars and beasts, and then God pauses over one creature and stamps it with his own likeness. The Latin phrase the church has carried for centuries is imago dei, the image of God. It is the foundation under every claim your civilization makes about human worth, and most people who depend on it have no idea it is there.

We should begin by feeling the strangeness of it, because the ancient world found it strange. In the cultures surrounding Israel, the image of a god was a statue housed in a temple, and the only human who bore the divine image was the king. Pharaoh was the image of the god. The peasant in the field was not. Then Genesis arrives and does something seismic. It takes the language reserved for the king and the temple statue and hands it to every human being without exception. Male and female. Slave and free. The dying infant and the failing elder. Gerhard von Rad, reading Genesis with care, saw that the image was not first about an internal quality but about a representative function, the human being placed in creation as God's regent, standing in for the king before the world (von Rad 1972). You are not a statue in a temple. You are a living likeness, set in the world to bear the face of the One who made it.

Now the objection, and it is a serious one, perhaps the most serious one a modern person can raise. The skeptic says human beings are not the image of anything. We are evolved primates, remarkable but not sacred, a temporary arrangement of matter that will dissolve. To call us images of God is a comforting fiction, and the honest view is that our worth is a story we tell ourselves to keep from despair. This objection is not crude. Its sharpest exponents, from Nietzsche forward, pressed it with terrible consistency. If God is dead, Nietzsche understood, then the dignity that was borrowed from God dies too, and we will have to invent our worth or admit we have none.

What the objection gets right is the dependency. It is correct that human dignity is borrowed, that it does not float free, that if you saw off the branch you are sitting on you will fall. The atheist philosopher who insists on universal human rights while denying any ground for them is living on inherited capital. Jurgen Habermas, no friend of the church, admitted that the idea of the equal worth of every person is a direct inheritance from the biblical doctrine of the image of God, and that secular reason has not produced a replacement, only continued to spend down the account (Habermas 2006). The skeptic is right that our dignity has a root. He is only wrong about whether the root is real. Cut the root, and you do not get a freestanding humanism. You get a managed humanity, sorted by usefulness, and the twentieth century showed us in detail what that sorting looks like.

Here is where the doctrine does its hardest work, because the image of God is not a flattering thing to be told. It is a weight before it is a comfort. If I bear the image of God, then so does the person I despise, and that is intolerable to the way I actually live. The doctrine indicts me before it dignifies my neighbor. James, the brother of Jesus, drives this exact point. With the tongue, he writes, 'we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God' (James 3:9 ESV). The same mouth. The contradiction James names is the contradiction in every one of us. We affirm human dignity in the abstract and assault it in the particular, in the driver who cut us off, in the relative we have written off, in the stranger whose politics we have decided makes him less. The image of God is not a doctrine that makes me feel good about humanity. It is a doctrine that convicts me of how casually I deface the likeness of God in the people I find inconvenient.

And this is where the story darkens before it heals, where the law comes before the grace. Because Genesis does not stop at chapter one. The image is given, and then the image is defaced. By chapter three the likeness is fractured, and by chapter four one image-bearer is murdering another in a field, and the rest of human history is the long record of the image of God lifting its hand against itself. We are not innocent statues. We are damaged ones, and the damage is not only out there in the violent. Augustine saw this with unflinching honesty, that the image in us is not erased but distorted, bent inward, curved away from the God it was made to reflect, so that we use the very faculties of likeness to grasp for ourselves (Augustine, On the Trinity). The image remains, which is why every human is sacred. The image is broken, which is why no human is safe.

Now the cross, and the cross is where the doctrine of the image is rescued from being merely a sentiment. The New Testament makes a claim that lands like a hammer. Jesus, it says, is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15 ESV). Not an image. The image. The likeness we were made to bear and shattered, he carries undamaged. And then he does the thing that turns the whole doctrine inside out. The true image of God is nailed to a cross by the defaced images of God, by us, and instead of destroying the ones defacing him, he dies to restore them. The image we ruined is repaired by the Image we killed. This is the grace, and it only makes sense after the law has done its diagnosis, after we have admitted that we are not merely image-bearers in need of affirmation but image-defacers in need of mercy.

Watch the reversal complete itself. The skeptic said our dignity is borrowed and therefore unreal. The gospel agrees that it is borrowed and insists that the lender came in person to make the loan good. We did not generate our worth and we cannot. It is given, and not only given at creation but given again at Calvary, where the cost of one defaced image is measured by what it took to restore it. The blood of the Son of God. That is the price tag the cross hangs on a human being. Whatever you think you are worth, the cross says you are worth the death of God to redeem. The skeptic worried our dignity was too cheap to be real. The gospel answers that it is too expensive to be anything but real.

So we go back into a world full of image-bearers, and the doctrine will not let us live the way we did. It abolishes the categories we use to rank people. There is no human being who is merely a means, merely a vote, merely a demographic, merely an obstacle. There is no one beneath your contempt because there is no one beneath God's likeness. James K.A. Smith reminds us that what we love and how we treat others is not first a matter of what we believe but of what we have been formed to desire, and that learning to see the image of God in the people we have been trained to overlook is a slow reformation of the heart, not a single decision (Smith 2009). You will not wake up tomorrow seeing every face as the face of a king's representative. But the cross has set the standard, and the standard does not bend.

This is what it means to bear the image of God. It means you are not an accident and you are not a product and you are not the sum of your usefulness. It means the dignity you hope is real is real, anchored not in your achievements but in your origin and bought back at your Maker's expense. And it means the person you most want to discount is carrying the same likeness, untouchable, redeemed at the same price. The doctrine that lifts you also strips you of the right to look down on anyone. You bear the image of God. So does everyone you were about to dismiss. Now go and treat them like it.

### Works Cited

Augustine of Hippo. On the Trinity. c. 416.

Habermas, Jurgen. Time of Transitions. Cambridge: Polity Press, 2006.

Smith, James K.A. Desiring the Kingdom: Worship, Worldview, and Cultural Formation. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2009.

von Rad, Gerhard. Genesis: A Commentary. Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1972.
